mappings.note: Interpreting Sri Aurobindo's line on India's early cultural unity from the Himalayas to the two seas asks the pupil to pull the chapter's strands together, which is the synthesis LO-90 names. Not LO-86, because the quotation is a modern statement about India, not a work of the ancient period.

A true/false set spanning what the Rig Veda, Vishnu Purana and Mahabharata actually say (LO-86) and what Persians and Greeks called India (LO-98). Both registers are tested, which no single outcome covers.
Invent a name you might have given the country 2,000 years ago: the pupil must draw together how the real names arose and why, which is synthesis rather than recall of any one text.
Why foreigners undertook long journeys to India - trade, pilgrimage, learning. That is the implication of India's contacts with regions outside it, which LO-98 names.
How today's India differs from the India of the past in name and borders - a synthesis across periods, so LO-90. Not LO-81, since no boundary has to be identified on a map.

'Indian Subcontinent' as the region covering India and its neighbours; LO-81 is the outcome that names India's neighbouring countries. Not LO-82, which is about mountains, plains and rivers inside India.

Identifies the Rig Veda as the text naming the north-west as Sapta Sindhava - content drawn from an ancient literary work, so LO-86. Not LO-84, because the item asks what the text says, not how texts serve as sources.
What 'Sindhu' meant in the Rig Veda (LO-86) and which river it names (LO-82). The item sits on both the text and the geography.
The Mahabharata as the epic listing Kashmira, Kurukshetra, Vanga and Pragjyotisha - a fact about the contents of an ancient literary work.
'Bharata' first appearing in the Rig Veda as a Vedic people; again what an ancient text contains, so LO-86 rather than the geography outcomes.
The literal sense of Jambudvipa, island of the jamun tree - a term carried by the ancient texts. Not LO-89, which is reserved here for the Ashokan inscriptions.
Names Ashoka as the emperor who used Jambudvipa in his edicts; LO-89 lists Ashokan inscriptions as its own example of a dynasty's contribution. Not LO-86, because inscriptions are not literary works.
The reach of Jambudvipa in Ashoka's day rests on the Ashokan inscriptions (LO-89) and on knowing which neighbouring countries it covered (LO-81).
Cape Kumari and the snowy mountain as the limits of the land show the texts' grasp of India's physical extent - LO-82 for the features, LO-86 for their being described in ancient works.

Article 1 of the Constitution, 'India, that is Bharat'. The Constitution belongs to CG-SST3; none of its outcomes, which deal with diversity, discrimination and local government, reaches the naming of the Union, so the goal is the honest altitude.
The Persians as the first outsiders to name the land Hind - a contact with a region outside India, which is LO-98. Not LO-86: no Indian text is involved.
Hind and Hindu as Persian adaptations of Sindhu; the mechanics of that borrowing are the implication of contact with Persia.
Greeks taking Indoi and Indike from Persian sources, not from Sanskrit - a two-step transmission between India and the world outside.
Chinese Yintu and Yindu, again traced back to Sindhu; the Chinese branch of the same contact story.
Tianzhu as 'heavenly master' reflecting Chinese regard for India as the home of Buddhism - explicitly the RELIGION field that LO-98 names.
Identifies Xuanzang as a Chinese Buddhist traveller who came to India for texts and teaching - a named contact with a region outside India.
'Hindustan' first attested in a Persian inscription; the item is about which outside language coined the name, so LO-98 rather than LO-84's source classification.
English 'India' descending from Greek Indike - the last link in the chain of foreign names, so LO-98.
Matches each ancient name to the people who used it and finds Hind with the Persians; a foreign-nomenclature item across the whole set.
Bharatavarsha as the indigenous name for the whole subcontinent, which the item asks a map maker to choose. It is an Indian textual name, so LO-86 rather than the foreign-contact outcome.
Finds the wrong gloss (Sapta Sindhava as land of seven seas) among the indigenous names and their meanings - textual vocabulary under LO-86.
Statement set mixing who really used 'Hindustan' and 'Indoi' (LO-98) with what the Constitution says (CG-SST3). The British claim in the stem is the one to be rejected.
Traces Hind, Indoi and India back to one river - the linguistic chain of outside contact (LO-98) anchored on the Indus (LO-82).

Maps the Mahabharata's Pragjyotisha onto modern Assam: locating an ancient place on the map of India (LO-85) from what an epic names (LO-86). This is the one item in the batch that needs the map outcome.
Dates Ashoka's reign to about 250 BCE, fixing when Jambudvipa is attested in his inscriptions - a fact about the Mauryan contribution named in LO-89.
Compares the scope of Bharatavarsha with Sapta Sindhava; both are textual names (LO-86) and the comparison is geographical (LO-82).
Pairs each foreign people with the name it used and settles on the Chinese Yintu - the foreign-nomenclature set, so LO-98.
Assertion-reason on 'India' evolving through Greek and Latin from Persian and Sanskrit; the reasoning is entirely about transmission outside India.
Finds 'Bharat - Chinese origin' as the false pairing, which requires knowing both the foreign names (LO-98) and that Bharat is Sanskrit and indigenous (LO-86).
Reads the sheer number of names as evidence of India's dealings with many cultures - the general statement of what LO-98 asks pupils to describe.
Sapta Sindhava as the land of seven rivers: a Rig Vedic term (LO-86) describing a river region (LO-82).
Jambudvipa named after the jamun tree - the indigenous term again, mapped with the other textual-name items and not with the Ashokan inscription ones.
Matches each ancient text to the name it uses and settles on the Mahabharata with Bharatavarsha; the sharpest of the text-to-name items, so LO-86.
A Greek writing of 'Indike' meant India - decoding a foreign name, hence LO-98.
Rejects 'Greeks coined Bharatavarsha' among claims about Xuanzang, the Persians and later invaders; wholly about who outside India used which name.
